zones.label: Column 1 running header
zones.note: Lexical aid: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510 (supplied page subset), CC BY 4.0. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Used for lexical identification after reading the scan, not as the authority for diplomatic spelling or typography. Lexical references are paraphrased in the English comments; the transcription was read independently from this scan.

lines.note: Continues the preceding explanation with the requirement for a negative verb. The example begins saseru koto de nai, something not important; the scan reads verbo, not the draft's verdo.
Nai completes the negative example, translated as not being a matter of importance. Roman l introduces an alternative, whose initial Sa- remains divided at this physical line ending.
Together with Sa- above, this gives saseranu koto ja. Idem assigns the same meaning to the alternative negative construction; cotogia retains the printed historical spelling.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de comer que ſe faz de ce-

lines.note: This noun sashi denotes a food preparation. The Portuguese starts ceuada, barley, across the line break; it is distinct from both the following plant-name homonym and the verb sasu.

runs.text: uada ainda noua, & piſada com ſal.

lines.note: Completes ceuada: the barley is still young and is pounded with salt. The gloss identifies the preparation without requiring a modern dish-name to be inserted.

runs.text: Hũas eruas ſecas, ou ſemẽte dellas q̃ ſe pega

lines.note: The second sashi denotes dried plants or their seeds that cling to clothing. The abbreviated semẽte and q̃ are preserved without expansion, and the space before ſe is visible.
The plants adhere strongly to garments; sashi ga toritsuku illustrates that sticking. The divided Portuguese Pe- belongs entirely to italic Pegarenſe, not a Japanese e fragment.
Completes Pegarenſe eſtas eruas, these plants sticking or attaching themselves. This short translation continuation is an independent physical row.
The verb gives the principal forms sashi, sasu, saita, initially glossed as pointing or showing. Aita is the historical s-row sound-change form and is not to be replaced with modern shita.
Yubi wo sasu means pointing with a finger. The next example begins A- and continues with meno below, forming ame no rather than a separate letter or abbreviation.

Continues ame no furu ga gotoku and describes aiming at the target, with zo marking the emphatic clause. The following Portuguese explains a shower of arrows; the printed yatçubo spelling is retained rather than modernized.

Itarikeru completes the archery quotation. The scan supports itariqeru rather than itartiqeru; the upright Taif. is a source label, followed by the italic book reference and the beginning of the translation, 'aiming'.

runs.text: com o arco no lugar onde queria dar, atirou tan-

lines.note: The translation describes aiming the bow at the intended point and shooting so many arrows. Atirou is visible, correcting alirou; tan- continues as tantas below.
The arrows were so numerous that they resembled rain; the relative word reads que, not quo. A new example, kasa wo sasu, begins at the end of the row.

runs.text: Empararſe com o ſombreiro alto do ſol, ou

lines.note: Completes kasa wo sasu, sheltering beneath a raised parasol or umbrella. The Portuguese empararſe spelling is retained, and this indented continuation is not a new entry.
Rain completes the sheltering sense. Katana wo saya ni sasu introduces putting a sword into its scabbard, with the Portuguese infinitive divided as Me-ter.

Completes the sword-and-scabbard translation. The following Japanese question asks toward where someone is going and continues below. Enlargement confirms Izzucuuo with doubled z, correcting the draft's Izucuuo without normalizing the historical spelling.
Completes the question 'Where are you heading?' Both the Japanese and Portuguese visibly end with question marks, not the draft's full stops. Fi- begins hi ga sasu below.

runs.text: Daro ſol em algũa parte, ou entrar

lines.note: Hi ga sasu describes sunlight falling on or entering a place. The close spacing in Daro is retained rather than silently recast as modern Dar o.
After completing the sunlight sense, fune ni sao wo sasu describes propelling a boat with a pole. The Portuguese Le- begins the corresponding verb leuar.
Leuar a Fune à vara means moving the boat by poling; Fune is a Japanese noun embedded in the Portuguese gloss. Ne wo sasu then introduces putting forth roots, with Lan- continuing below.
Completes lançar raizes, producing roots. Makage wo sasu begins the gesture explained by the following line: placing the hand above the eyes to shade them.

runs.text: mão ſobre os olhos pera ver milhor ao longe.

lines.note: The hand shades the eyes to improve distant vision. The historical spellings pera and milhor are preserved; this is the completion of the makage example, not a separate sense-heading.
Nekki ga sasu is illustrated as the onset or appearance of fever. The Portuguese medical wording is the historical dictionary's gloss, not a modern clinical assertion.
Sakazuki wo sasu is explained as sending or offering the drinking cup to someone else. The Portuguese object continues onto the following row.
Sacazzuqui completes the Portuguese cup-gloss and is an embedded Japanese term. Todome wo sasu, alternatively utsu, then introduces administering a finishing blow; v- continues as tçu.

runs.text: Acabar de matar ao que começa a mor-

lines.note: Completes utsu. The translation describes finishing the killing of someone already beginning to die; its context is completed by por juſtiça on the next row.
Completes the execution-context gloss for todome. Sen wo sasu then means inserting a stopper or plugging an opening, whose Portuguese object follows below.
Torno completes the stopper example. Shio ga sasu introduces the incoming tide; the Portuguese noun for tide is deferred to the next row.

Marè completes the rising-tide sense; its visible accent is retained as grave rather than the draft's tilde. Tori wo sasu begins a bird-catching example, and no extra full stop follows the paragraph sign.

runs.text: com ponta de bambu enuiſcado. ¶ Item,

lines.note: The birds are caught with a birdlime-coated bamboo tip. The scan supports bambu, not hambu; Item introduces another sense on the next line.

runs.text: Morder a cobra, picar a abelha, moſ-

lines.note: Sasu is now illustrated by a snake's bite and the stings or bites of insects. The final moſ- belongs to Portuguese mosquito across the physical break.
Completes mosquito and gives hachi ga sasu, a bee stinging. The Portuguese subject of picar continues below, maintaining the same example.
After completing the bee example, the gloss turns to delivering a sword thrust. Eſtocada is entirely Portuguese italic, not a roman ocada fragment; Na- starts nanakatana.

Nanakatana made saita is translated as giving someone seven sword thrusts. Saita is the same historical past form supplied in the headword, not the flower-blooming verb suggested by modern sound alone.
Catana completes the sword-thrust translation and is a Japanese loan term inside Portuguese. Tatami wo sasu begins the separate sense of making or stitching tatami mats.
Tatamis are glossed as straw mattresses or mats; the Japanese pluralized noun occurs within Portuguese. The scan's nasalized ending in colchoẽs is retained, and Ficari- begins hikari ga sasu.
Hikari ga sasu means emitting or giving off light; the scan has ga ſaſu, not gaiſaſu. Hari sa- begins the next needle-space expression.
Completes hari sasu hodo mo nai, having not even room for a needle. The Portuguese a- is the beginning of ainda on the following row, not a separate article.

runs.text: inda quanto ſe pode tocar com hũa agulha.

lines.note: Completes the explanation of the extremely small space: not even enough to touch with a needle. The separate physical line is preserved although it only continues the preceding translation.
Iremono, hako nado wo sasu gives the joinery sense of making containers or boxes. Fazer introduces the Portuguese objects on the next row.

runs.text: algũa caixa, ou boceta, ou outra couſa ſemelhãte.

lines.note: The objects are a box, small case, or something similar. This completes the last example under the long sasu entry; the enlarged scan confirms the nasal abbreviation ſemelhãte, which is retained without expansion.
Sashiage, sashiaguru, sashiageta means raising something with the hand. This begins a new compound-verb entry, distinct from the many senses of sasu above.
Hata wo sashiaguru illustrates raising or hoisting flags. Portuguese bandeiras is visibly divided after ban-.
Completes bandeiras, the flags being raised. The short row is genuine body text, not a catchword or removable fragment.

runs.text: O encontrarſe, ou conuerſar com ou-

lines.note: Sashiai denotes meeting or conversing with another person. Its initial is S, correcting the draft's B; ou- continues as outro rather than introducing another alternative here.
Completes outro and gives sashiai no yoi hito, someone pleasant to converse with. The damaged but recoverable fito replaces fto, restoring the ordinary Japanese word for a person.
Completes Homem de boa conuerſação, a person of good conversation. The line is indented like other continuations, not set as a fresh headword.
This verbal sashiai means being occupied with necessary matters. The principal parts retain their carons; ne- begins the Portuguese adjective completed below.
Completes neceßarias and gives hima ga sashiyoo, having one's time occupied. The visibly printed ſaxiyǒ is retained rather than assimilated to the headword spelling.

runs.text: cupado, ou não ter tempo, nem vagar.

lines.note: Completes occupado and paraphrases the example as having neither time nor leisure. Vagar here is leisure, not the verb 'to wander'.
The noun sashiai is an impediment or occupation. Its scan reading is Saxiai, not Saxſai; the example begins 'this' and continues with a linked-verse composition.
Kono renga ni wa sashiai ga ooi refers to numerous faults or constraints in a linked verse. The printed vouoi is preserved rather than normalized.

runs.text: ou verſo ha muitos erros, quebras, ou faltas.

lines.note: The translation specifies many errors, breaks, or faults in the verse. The scan has doubled r in erros, correcting the draft's eros.
Sashiatari, sashiataru in its abbreviated paradigm, concerns necessity or relevance here. The Portuguese perten- continues as pertencer; the written principal forms are left unexpanded.
The example advises postponement unless the matter is immediately pressing. Naquua and imperative nobei are retained as printed historical forms, without modern grammatical respelling.

runs.text: Se não for couſa muito importante dilatai.

lines.note: The Portuguese explicitly says to delay it unless it is a very important matter. Dilatai supplies the imperative force of nobei above.
Sashiatatte is glossed as particularly or in a particular case. This independent adverbial entry should not be merged into the preceding verb paradigm.
Completes caso particular. This one-word physical row closes the adverbial gloss and is not page furniture.

Sashiatsumari concerns people gathering together. The scan restores Saxiatçumari and Ajuntarſe; the printed ru principal-part abbreviation is retained even though a different abbreviation might be expected.
The people gather from various places. This completes the preceding gathering verb rather than introducing another entry.
Sashiate means touching or addressing something by pointing. The principal form tçuru belongs to the historical verb paradigm and is retained.
The example applies the verb to giving pointed advice. The Portuguese mani- begins manifestamente, expressing directness rather than concealment.
Completes manifestamente: openly and without circumlocution. The gloss explains the figurative force of the advice example above.
Sashiategai is aiming or pointing. Tep- begins teppoo, the gun in the following example; the printed carons remain distinct from its circumflex.
Teppoo wo sashiategoote hanasu describes aiming the gun and firing. The contracted historical form ſaxiategǒte and abbreviated Portuguese cõ are preserved.
Completes the instruction-like example as firing after aiming the gun. Deſparar is the dictionary's Portuguese spelling, not modernized to disparar.
Sashiawase means bringing one thing together with another. The scan supports Saxiauaxe, matching the example below, and Ajuntar rather than Ajuantar.
Completes 'with another' and starts an example about various difficulties occurring together. Mutçuca- continues as the adjective mutçucaxij on the next row.
The troublesome matters come crowding in together. Qiſoi qitaru is retained as printed; Portuguese mui- begins muitas and is not a Japanese fragment.
Many things accumulating cause many complications to arise. This closes the Portuguese explanation of the combined-difficulties example.
Sashiba is glossed simply as a small hawk or falcon. No modern species identification is imposed on the historical Portuguese description.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de coco com cabo

lines.note: Sashibishaku is a handled dipper, described by comparison with a coconut-shell vessel. The handle and carrying method distinguish the implement in the continuation.

runs.text: pera tirar, ou tomar agoa, que ſe leua na cinta.

lines.note: It is used to draw or take water and is carried at the waist. The gloss describes the dipper's use, not a second headword.
Sashikakari means being above or overhanging. The final de- belongs to dependurado on the next row; it is not an isolated preposition.
Completes the description as hanging above or about to fall. Ki no begins an example about the branches of a tree.
The branches overhang the water. The scan appears to print mizzuni with doubled z; that local spelling is retained rather than normalized to the draft's mizuni.

runs.text: mos daruore ſaidos, ou caidos ſobre a agoa

lines.note: Completes ramos: the tree's branches project or droop over the water. No final full stop is supplied where the scan does not clearly print one.
Sashikamae is waiting or being in readiness. The example following this new headword specifies people who were waiting.
Sashikamayetaru ninju means a group that was waiting. The historical attributive taru and abbreviated q̃ are left unchanged.

runs.text: O fazer algũa maneira de caſa toſ-

lines.note: Sashikake denotes making a rough kind of shelter or house. Toſ- begins toſca in the Portuguese description across the break.
The construction is crude and imperfect. Sashikake wo starts the example whose light verb is on the next short line.
Suru completes sashikake wo suru, making the rough shelter. This single-word continuation is genuine body text and keeps its own crop and ID.
Sashikarami means surrounding or enclosing. The Portuguese cõ introduces the people used to form the cordon, explained in the following lines.

runs.text: gente pera que não fuja alguem, &c. Vt,

lines.note: The enclosure uses people so that someone cannot escape. This completes the definition before its example, rather than identifying a physical fence.
Happoo wo ninju de sashikaramu means surrounding all sides with people. The faint mark over the o in Fappôuo is provisionally read as a circumflex from the local scan.
Completes the translation as surrounding every side with people. The line belongs to the cordon example above.

runs.text: Sombreiro de mão pera o ſol, ou

lines.note: Sashikasa is a hand-held parasol or umbrella. The gloss contrasts protection from sun with protection from rain on the next line.
Rain completes the umbrella definition. Its brevity does not make it furniture or justify merging away the physical row.
Sashikata describes conspicuously raised shoulders. The Portuguese wording is a historical evaluative description of the bodily feature.
Sashikata no hito means someone with that shoulder shape. The scan reads Homem without the draft's extra t; de- starts deformidade.
Completes the description of protruding or raised shoulders. The worn middle letters support eminentes, not the draft's emmentes.
Sashikatame means arming oneself or putting on armour. Vestir continues with its object armas below.
The example names kote and kogusoku, arm protection and associated armour, before the divided verb sashikatameta. The Japanese list remains roman.

Completes sashikatameta. The translation mentions taking the arm defences and gorget or collar; golla corrects gilla. The sentence continues with armouſe at the start of f0442, while its repetition below is a catchword.
